opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is this. When a model is reasoning, say producing a chain of thought before it makes a prediction, you want some way to tell whether that reasoning actually helped. Information gain gives you a natural handle on that. You ask: after the model generates this thought, how much more confident did it become about the right answer, or about the actual next text, compared to before? If the reasoning raised the likelihood of what really comes next, that's useful information. If it didn't move anything, or made things worse, then it was just filler, or even misleading.

What I find appealing is that it's a fairly intrinsic signal. You don't necessarily need a human labeling every step as good or bad, and you don't need a verifier that only works for math or code where there's a crisp right answer. You can apply it to ordinary text. In a sense you're rewarding the model for thinking in ways that make the world less surprising to it, which is close to what we mean by understanding.

I'd add a few caveats, though. Information gain measured through the model's own probabilities depends on how well calibrated the model is, so you have to watch for the model gaming its own uncertainty. And not everything valuable in reasoning shows up immediately as a likelihood bump. Some thoughts pay off later, or matter for robustness rather than accuracy. So I see it less as the one true reward and more as a principled, scalable starting point, especially for pushing reasoning beyond the narrow domains where we already have verifiable rewards.

r001.rationale: The response describes information gain as making the actual answer or next text less surprising, not as maximizing surprise in predictions.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that information-gain rewards favor predictive diversity over improved accuracy; it frames them as rewarding increased likelihood of the correct answer or actual next text.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really fascinating. The way I think about it is, when a model makes a prediction, you can ask: how much did that prediction actually reduce my uncertainty about the world? That's information gain in the Shannon sense. And the interesting move is to turn that into a reward signal, rather than just rewarding the model for being right.

Because if you only reward correctness, you get a model that's very good at saying obvious things. It learns to predict the next token that's most likely, and most of the time, the most likely token is not very informative. It's the "the" and the "of" and the safe, generic continuation. So you end up with this kind of blandness that we all recognize in language model outputs.

Information gain as a reward flips that a bit. You're saying, I don't just want you to be right, I want you to tell me something I didn't already know, or couldn't have easily guessed. So you compare the model's belief before and after seeing the prediction, or you compare it against some baseline model, and the reward is the delta. The more surprising and still correct the prediction, the higher the reward.

Now, there's a tension here that I think is really important, and it's the tension between surprise and truth. Surprise alone is cheap. I can be very surprising by saying nonsense. So information gain only works as a reward if it's grounded in some verification, some notion that the surprising thing was also right. Otherwise you're just training a model to hallucinate confidently, which is the last thing we want.

And the other thing I'd say is that this connects to how humans learn, actually. Children don't learn by being told the most likely thing. They learn by being surprised, by having their predictions violated, and then updating. Curiosity-driven learning in developmental psychology is very much about seeking out exactly the inputs that maximize your information gain. So there's something cognitively natural about it, even though in the language model setting we have to be careful about the mechanics.

So that's roughly how I understand it: reward the model for predictions that are both correct and non-obvious, measured by how much they shift what you believe. It's a way of pushing models toward being genuinely informative rather than merely plausible.

r001.rationale: The response describes rewarding predictions that reduce uncertainty and explicitly says more surprising, correct predictions receive higher reward.

r002.rationale: It contrasts information gain with rewarding correctness alone, but does not say that such rewards may favor predictive diversity.

astra-6.text:
I think of information gain as how much a prediction changes what you know. If a model predicts something that was already obvious from the context, then getting it right doesn’t give you much new information. But if it correctly predicts something that was uncertain, that can be much more informative.

The important distinction is between being informative and simply being surprising. A random, nonsensical answer can be surprising, but that doesn’t make it useful. So if we use information gain as a reward, we need to ask: whose uncertainty are we reducing, and about what? Ideally, we’re rewarding predictions that help us arrive at a better understanding, rather than just predictions that are unusual.

r001.rationale: The response describes information gain as reducing uncertainty and distinguishes that from mere surprise; it does not interpret it as maximizing surprise.

r002.rationale: It cautions against rewarding unusual predictions, but does not say information-gain rewards favor predictive diversity over improved prediction accuracy.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that the model should get credit for how much its prediction reduces uncertainty, rather than simply for predicting something that was already very likely. If I tell you something obvious, you haven’t learned much. But if I tell you something you didn’t expect that helps you understand what comes next, that has more information value.

The tricky part is that being surprising is not enough. A random or incorrect statement can also be surprising. So you want the reward to capture useful information—something that improves your predictions or your understanding—not just novelty.

r001.rationale: The response connects information value to surprise and uncertainty reduction, but says surprise alone is insufficient and frames the reward around useful information rather than maximizing surprise.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that information-gain rewards favor predictive diversity over accuracy; it says useful information should improve predictions or understanding.
